ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two thermally conductive cylinders, facing each other and fixed at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, are connected at the bottom by a thin tube with negligible volume. The cross-sectional areas of pistons $a$ and $b$ are $S_{1}=10\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ and $S_{2}=20\mathrm{cm}^{2}$, respectively. The total mass of the two pistons is $m=12\mathrm{kg}$, and the height of both cylinders is $H=10\mathrm{cm}$. The cylinders contain a certain amount of ideal gas, and when the system is in equilibrium, the distances from pistons $a$ and $b$ to the bottom of the cylinders are both $L=5\mathrm{cm}$. The atmospheric pressure is $p_{0}=1.0{\times}10^{5}\mathrm{Pa}$, the ambient temperature is $T_{0}=300\mathrm{K}$, and the gravitational acceleration $g$ is taken as $10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. If the ambient temperature remains constant, and a force is applied slowly upward along the light rod to push piston $a$, what is the maximum value of the thrust during the process from the start of the movement of piston $a$ until it reaches the bottom of the cylinder?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: The diagram shows two inclined cylinders whose axes lie along a line making 30° with the horizontal. The two cylinders face each other, with piston b in the left cylinder and piston a in the right cylinder. Each cylinder has marked length H, and the lower ends are connected by a thin tube, so the gas in both cylinders communicates. The geometry implies that when the connected pistons move along their common light rod, piston a moves toward its own bottom while piston b moves away from its own bottom, i.e. their gas-volume changes are opposite in sign. Reasoning: Let ΔS = S2 − S1. Numerically, S1 = 10 cm² = 1.0×10^-3 m², S2 = 20 cm² = 2.0×10^-3 m², so ΔS = 1.0×10^-3 m². Initially no external thrust is applied, and the two-piston-plus-rod system is in equilibrium along the incline. According to the assigned force balance, the pressure-force difference balances the downslope component of the total piston weight: (p_i − p0)ΔS = mg sin30°. Here mg sin30° = 12×10×1/2 = 60 N. Thus p_i − p0 = 60/(1.0×10^-3) = 6.0×10^4 Pa, so p_i = 1.0×10^5 + 6.0×10^4 = 1.6×10^5 Pa. Let x be the displacement of piston a toward the bottom of its cylinder. Because the pistons move oppositely, the gas length in cylinder a becomes L − x, while that in cylinder b becomes L + x. Therefore the gas volume is V(x) = S1(L − x) + S2(L + x) = (S1 + S2)L + (S2 − S1)x = V0 + ΔS x. Initially V0 = (S1 + S2)L = (10 + 20)cm² × 5cm = 150 cm³. The cylinders are thermally conductive and the ambient temperature is constant, so the gas undergoes an isothermal process: p(x)V(x) = p_i V0, therefore p(x) = p_i V0/V(x). The quasi-static force balance with applied upward thrust F is F + (p − p0)ΔS = mg sin30°, so F(x) = mg sin30° − (p(x) − p0)ΔS. Since V(x) increases with x, p(x) decreases with x, so F(x) increases with x. Hence the maximum thrust occurs when piston a just reaches the bottom, x = L. At x = L, the final gas volume is V_f = S1(L − L) + S2(L + L) = S2H = 20cm² × 10cm = 200 cm³. Thus p_f = p_i V0/V_f = 1.6×10^5 × 150/200 = 1.2×10^5 Pa. Then F_max = 60 − (1.2×10^5 − 1.0×10^5)(1.0×10^-3) = 60 − 20 = 40 N.
